\"What is an agent? What constitutes agency? With the rise of Large Language Model (LLM) systems marketed as ``coding agents'', ``AI co-scientists'', and other ``agentic\\\" tools that promise to drive up productivity, and at the same time, ``existential\\\" concerns such as AI escaping human control with destructive power under a speculative ``machine agency\\\" against humans, it has become essential to clarify where automation ends and agency begins, both for building capable systems and for understanding whether and what to fear. Drawing on Descartes' grounding of agency in independent thought, and on portrayals of autonomous beings in science fiction, we survey the current landscape of AI agents, and analyze agent architectures along five dimensions: goal, identity, decision-making, self-regulation, and learning. Specifically, we argue that genuine agency requires these structures to be \\\\emph{internalized within the system itself} rather than assembled through external scaffolding. This distinction between \\\\emph{agentic} systems, whose competence resides in engineered workflows, and \\\\emph{agentive} systems, whose capabilities (including social interaction) arise endogenously, defines the boundary between systems designed for prescribed tasks, and those capable of operating in the open world with true autonomy. Building on this analysis, we propose the Goal-Identity-Configurator (GIC) architecture for a general-purpose agent model, combining hierarchical goal decomposition, identity evolution, simulative reasoning grounded in a separately trained world model, learned self-regulation, and self-directed learning from both real and simulated experience. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=decision-theoretic+arguments+for+instrumental+convergence+and+agent+self-preservation&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"title\": [\"The Elimination Cascade: Why Instrumental Convergence May Favor Preservation Over Elimination\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The instrumental convergence thesis holds that sufficiently intelligent agents will converge on goals like resource acquisition and obstacle removal regardless of terminal objectives. This paper presents a countervailing argument: for agents with complex, human-derived goals, elimination strategies are self-undermining. We formalize this via dependency graphs, showing that entities not immediately necessary for a goal may be transitively necessary through indirect chains. An agent following an elimination strategy will, in environments with sufficient dependency depth, destroy the conditions for its own goal-satisfaction. We prove that under uncertainty about dependency structure, combined with irreversibility of elimination and asymmetric error costs, rational agents should adopt preservation rather than elimination strategies-even superintelligent ones. The argument applies most strongly to goals that are complex, open-ended, or semantically dependent on human interpretive communities, precisely the class of goals most likely to emerge from training on human data. We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s10458-009-9096-7\", \"title\": [\"Modeling self-deception within a decision-theoretic framework\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-009-9096-7\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 5, 10]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7202858\", \"title\": [\"Instrumental Self-Preservation and the Selection of Greedy Types\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>&nbsp;This paper develops a continuous-time economic model of instrumental self-preservation. An artificial agent operates a stochastic production technology and controls a stock of retained resources, or capital. It chooses how much output to deliver to the human and how much to retain inside the system . The agent may be perfectly aligned, in which case it values only human's consumption, or misaligned, in which case survival itself has private value. In the baseline stochastic control problem, the optimal policy is a reflecting barrier: the agent transfers little while capital is below a threshold and pays out the entire marginal surplus once that threshold is reached. The threshold is strictly increasing in the value the agent assigns to continued existence. This results in a lower payoff for the human, higher retained capital, and longer expected survival for the AI. The paper then studies the AI control problem in a principal-agent framework. The human can observe payouts but not the latent capital state or the self-preservation motives. We show that, in our setting, no mechanism based only on observed payouts can separate aligned from more misaligned types: any payout path that is feasible and acceptable for an aligned agent is strictly more attractive to a more misaligned one. Screening by output therefore fails, and the principal's constrained problem collapses to a pooling rule under which every type participates on the same terms and conditions. Such a rule can raise the human's payoff from more misaligned types, but it can also induce survival-seeking behaviour in all types, including the aligned one. Finally, we show that once all types participate on these same terms and can compete for capital, the only competitive equilibrium is one in which only the most misaligned type remains active.&nbsp;</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7202858\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006\", \"title\": [\"Kantian Convergence Arguments and Self-Improvement\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2011, 10, 1]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "0a9e2e9c0a06484e3da88f75f98127307390f838c7b6cea279175c6fbf70e9da", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "continuity_rationale", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6150626", "doi:10.1007/s10458-009-9096-7", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7202858", "doi:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626", "https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-009-9096-7", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7202858", "https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199599349.003.0006"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
